worksheet.title: Write the Steps
worksheet.subtitle: Write the algorithm in order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can write the steps of a task in the right order.

parts.title: Write an algorithm
parts.text: Writing an algorithm means writing the steps in order. Use the step bank to write the steps for brushing your teeth in the right order. Then write your own algorithm.

parts.title: Brush your teeth — step bank (mixed up)
Write the steps in order
parts.prompt: Write the four steps in the right order on the lines (you can use the letters). Step 1 first, down to step 4.

parts.title: Why this order?
parts.prompt: Which step must be FIRST? Could you brush before you put on toothpaste? Tell why the order matters.

parts.title: You try — write your own
parts.prompt: Write your own algorithm: how do you get ready for bed? Write 3 or 4 steps in order, one per line.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: When you write the steps of a task in the right order, you have written an algorithm. A good algorithm has each step where it needs to be.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students write an algorithm: they order a step bank into the steps for brushing teeth, explain why that order is needed, then write their own bedtime algorithm. Writing the ordered steps of a task is creating a sequential algorithm (C3.1); explaining why the order matters is C3.2.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: cut the step bank apart so students can arrange the cards before copying them onto the lines.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: read the step bank. 'I write the FIRST step on line 1 — wet the brush — then keep going.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — write wet the brush, put on toothpaste, brush your teeth, rinse your mouth (B, D, A, C). Exercise 2 — first is 'wet the brush'; toothpaste must come before brushing.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — students write their own 3-4 step bedtime algorithm in order.
4. Connect: 'Writing the steps in order is writing code — coders plan the order so the job works.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Brush your teeth in order: wet the brush (B), put on toothpaste (D), brush your teeth (A), rinse your mouth (C).
Ex 2 — 'Wet the brush' must be first; you cannot brush before the toothpaste is on, so put on toothpaste comes before brush your teeth. Swapping them breaks the algorithm.

Ex 3 — open. A sample bedtime algorithm: put on pyjamas, brush your teeth, read a book, turn off the light. Accept any 3-4 steps in a sensible order (an action that depends on another comes after it).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip in Ex 3: steps with no clear order — ask 'which one has to happen before another?' to surface dependencies.
Simplify: give a starter step bank for the bedtime task instead of a blank write.
Extend: ask students to trade algorithms with a partner and follow each other's steps to test them.
Success indicator: the child writes B, D, A, C for brushing and a sensible, correctly-ordered bedtime algorithm.
